solution:
Throughout, use the first law in the form the chapter states it, \(\Delta U = Q - W\), where \(Q\) is the heat **supplied to** the system (positive when energy enters the system) and \(W\) is the work done **by** the system on its surroundings (positive when the system expands).

**(a) Has there been a transfer of heat? No.** \(Q = 0\), so this is an **adiabatic** compression. Two separate reasons make it so, and here both apply at once:

1. the thick layer of insulating material seals the cylinder thermally, so no heat can cross the boundary; and
2. the compression is **quick**, so even an imperfect insulator would leave the gas no time to exchange heat with its surroundings.

**(b) Has work been done? Yes.** The piston is pushed in, so the volume of the gas decreases. Work is done **on** the gas by the agent compressing it; since \(W\) is defined as the work done *by* the system, \(W\) is **negative** here.

**What follows from the two answers together.** Putting \(Q = 0\) into the first law,

\(\Delta U = 0 - W = -W\)

and as \(W\) is negative, \(\Delta U\) is **positive**. The internal energy of the gas **increases**, and therefore its temperature **rises** — even though not a joule of heat was supplied to it. All the work done on the gas has gone into its internal energy. This is why adiabatic compression causes heating of a system, and it is exactly what makes the fuel in a diesel engine hot enough to ignite without a spark plug.

A process in which **no heat is added to or removed from** the system is an **adiabatic process**: \(Q = 0\). The first law then reduces to

\(\Delta U = -W\)

so the internal energy — and hence the temperature — changes purely because of the work done, with no heat crossing the boundary at all. Heat exchange is prevented either by insulating the system, or by making the change so **sudden** that there is no time to exchange heat.

**Example 1 — puncturing an inflated tyre or a balloon (cooling).** The compressed air rushes out and expands so rapidly that no heat can be exchanged with the surroundings, so \(Q = 0\). The escaping air does positive work in pushing back the atmosphere, so \(W\) is positive and \(\Delta U = -W\) is **negative**. The internal energy falls and the air **cools** noticeably, which is why the air escaping from a punctured tyre feels cold.

**Example 2 — the compression stroke of a diesel engine (heating).** The fuel and air mixture in the cylinder is compressed so quickly that \(Q = 0\). Work is done **on** the gas, so \(W\) is negative and \(\Delta U = -W\) is **positive**. The temperature of the mixture rises so high that the fuel ignites without any spark plug.

The two examples are the two directions of the same effect: **adiabatic expansion causes cooling and adiabatic compression causes heating**, in both cases with no heat added or removed.

A process in which the temperature stays constant is an **isothermal process** (\(\Delta T = 0\)). Heat can be supplied to a system throughout such a process, so heat added and temperature raised are **not** the same thing.

**Example 1 — a change of phase: melting of ice, or boiling of water.** Ice at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is supplied heat continuously, yet stays at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) until the last of it has melted; water boiling at atmospheric pressure stays at \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\) while it is all turning into steam. Any change of phase occurs at a constant temperature and is therefore an isothermal process. The heat supplied (the latent heat) is not used to speed up the molecules — it is spent in breaking the bonding between them, and in doing the work of the volume change that accompanies the change of state. Since none of it goes into raising the molecular kinetic energy, the thermometer does not move.

**Example 2 — isothermal expansion of a gas.** Let a gas in a cylinder be in good thermal contact with its surroundings and be allowed to expand very slowly, so that thermal equilibrium is maintained throughout. Then \(\Delta T = 0\), and because the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, \(\Delta U = 0\). The first law \(\Delta U = Q - W\) then gives

\(Q = W\)

so **all** the heat supplied is converted into the work done by the gas in expanding, and none of it is left over to raise the temperature.

The efficiency of a heat engine is the fraction of the absorbed heat that is converted into work,

\(\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_H} = 1 - \dfrac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}\)

where \(Q_H\) is the heat absorbed from the source and \(Q_C\) the heat rejected to the sink. Three separate things set limits on it.

**1. Heat is always rejected to the sink, so \(\eta\) is never 1.** Ideally we would want the engine to convert the whole of \(Q_H\) into work. In practice this never happens: some heat is always lost, that is \(Q_C \neq 0\), so \(|Q_C| / |Q_H|\) is never zero and \(\eta\) is always **less than 100%**.

**2. The fundamental limit is the second law of thermodynamics.** The first law does not forbid a perfect engine — it is merely a statement that heat and work are equivalent, and it would happily allow all the heat to be turned into work. It is the **second law** that rules this out. In its Kelvin-Planck (engine) form: *it is impossible to extract an amount of heat \(Q_H\) from a hot reservoir and use it all to do work \(W\); some amount of heat \(Q_C\) must be exhausted to a cold reservoir.* Hence a heat engine of 100% efficiency cannot be built, however well it is designed.

**3. The numerical ceiling is set by the two reservoir temperatures alone.** The largest efficiency any engine working between a source at \(T_H\) and a sink at \(T_C\) can have is the efficiency of a completely reversible (Carnot) cycle,

\(\eta_{\max} = 1 - \dfrac{T_C}{T_H}\)

with the temperatures in kelvin. For example, an engine that receives heat at \(800\) K and rejects it at \(400\) K can have a maximum efficiency of only \(50\%\), no matter what working substance or mechanism is used.

**4. A real engine falls further below even this.** The Carnot value assumes every step is reversible. Friction and other irreversible processes in an actual engine reduce its efficiency below \(\eta_{\max}\).

**Consequence for design:** since \(\eta_{\max} = 1 - T_C / T_H\), the source temperature \(T_H\) should be made as high as possible and the sink temperature \(T_C\) as low as possible.

A Carnot engine is the hypothetical engine of **maximum efficiency**, and an engine can convert the maximum possible heat into work only if **every step of its cycle is reversible**. So the question becomes: what must each step be, for it to be reversible? A cycle needs only two kinds of step, and each kind forces one answer.

**(i) The steps in which heat is exchanged must be ISOTHERMAL.** For heat exchange to be reversible there must be no finite temperature difference across which the heat flows — heat crossing a finite temperature gap is a spontaneous, one-way, irreversible process. So while the working substance absorbs \(Q_H\) it must be at the temperature \(T_H\) of the source, and while it rejects \(Q_C\) it must be at the temperature \(T_C\) of the sink. A process carried out at a constant temperature is an isothermal process. Hence **two isothermal steps** are needed, one at \(T_H\) and one at \(T_C\).

**(ii) The steps in which the temperature changes must be ADIABATIC.** The working substance still has to be carried from \(T_H\) down to \(T_C\) and back again. During these steps no heat may be exchanged, because heat exchange while the temperature is changing would necessarily occur across a finite temperature difference and so would be irreversible. A process in which no heat is exchanged (\(Q = 0\)) is an adiabatic process, and the temperature change is then produced by the work done alone. Hence **two adiabatic steps**.

**The cycle that results.** The four steps in order are: **A to B** isothermal expansion at \(T_H\), absorbing \(Q_H\); **B to C** adiabatic expansion, cooling the substance from \(T_H\) to \(T_C\); **C to D** isothermal compression at \(T_C\), rejecting \(Q_C\); and **D to A** adiabatic compression, warming it back from \(T_C\) to \(T_H\) and closing the cycle. Two isothermal and two adiabatic processes are therefore not a choice but a requirement, and they give the maximum possible efficiency

\(\eta = 1 - \dfrac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|} = 1 - \dfrac{T_C}{T_H}\)

Take the enclosed mixture of hydrogen and oxygen as the **system**; the cylinder is its boundary and everything outside is the environment. Read the two properties of that cylinder one at a time.

**The cylinder is rigid, so \(W = 0\).** The volume cannot change, so \(\Delta V = 0\) and \(W = p\,\Delta V = 0\). No work is done by the system on its surroundings, and none is done on it. (This is the isochoric condition: a system does no work on its environment during a constant-volume change.)

**The cylinder is insulating, so \(Q = 0\).** No heat can cross the boundary in either direction, which is the adiabatic condition. The spark's energy is given as negligible, so nothing else enters either.

**Apply the first law.**

\(\Delta U = Q - W = 0 - 0 = 0\)

**Conclusion 1 — the internal energy of the system does not change**, even though the temperature and the pressure both rise considerably. The system is effectively an *isolated* system: matter, heat and work are all barred from crossing its boundary, so its total energy content is fixed.

**Conclusion 2 — the energy that raised the temperature came from inside the system, not from outside.** Since no energy entered, the rise in temperature can only be a **conversion of energy from one form to another within the system**. The mixture already held energy stored chemically in its hydrogen and oxygen molecules; on ignition that stored energy is converted into the random, disordered kinetic energy of the molecules of the product, and it is precisely that disordered molecular energy which a rise in temperature measures. The total internal energy is unchanged; only its form has changed. The pressure rises with the temperature because the volume is held fixed.

**Conclusion 3 — a caution about when the law may be applied.** During the explosion itself the temperature and pressure are not uniform through the cylinder, so the mixture is *not* in an equilibrium state and cannot be described by state variables at all. The first law may therefore be applied only between the **initial** equilibrium state (before the spark) and the **final** equilibrium state (after the products have settled to a uniform temperature and pressure), not to the intermediate stages.

The **system is the resistor**; the running water and the electrical source are its environment. Keep to the convention \(\Delta U = Q - W\), with \(Q\) the heat supplied **to** the system and \(W\) the work done **by** the system.

**(a) Does heat flow into the resistor? No — heat flows out of it.** The current makes the resistor hotter than the water flowing over it. Heat is, by definition, the energy transferred between a system and its environment *because of a temperature difference between the two*, and that difference here drives energy from the hotter resistor to the cooler water. So heat leaves the resistor and \(Q\) is **negative** for the system.

**(b) Is there a flow of heat into the water? Yes.** The water is the environment into which the resistor's heat flows, so for the water the same transfer counts as heat gained. The water is *running*, so it continuously carries that heat away and keeps the resistor's temperature from climbing.

**(c) Is any work done? Yes.** The electrical source drives a current through the resistor and thereby does **electrical work on** the resistor. This transfer is *work* and not heat, because it does not take place through a temperature difference. As \(W\) denotes the work done *by* the system, \(W\) is **negative** here.

**(d) Apply the first law.** The state of the resistance is unchanged — the resistor stays at the same temperature and in the same condition — so its internal energy does not change:

\(\Delta U = 0\)

Hence

\(\Delta U = Q - W \Rightarrow 0 = Q - W \Rightarrow Q = W\)

Both quantities are negative, so in magnitude \(|Q| = |W|\).

**What this means physically:** every joule of electrical work done on the resistor leaves it again as exactly one joule of heat delivered to the water. The resistor stores none of it — it simply acts as a converter of electrical work into heat, and the running water removes that heat as fast as it is produced. This is a steady state, not an accumulation.

Take the **mixture of fuel and oxygen** as the system; the constant-volume chamber is its boundary and the water bath around it is the environment. Use \(\Delta U = Q - W\), with \(Q\) the heat supplied **to** the system and \(W\) the work done **by** the system.

**(a) Has heat been transferred? Yes — out of the system.** The observation given is that the temperature of the *water* increased. The water can only have gained that energy from the burning mixture, across the chamber wall, driven by the temperature difference between the two. So heat has flowed from the system to its environment, and for the system

\(Q\) is **negative**.

**(b) Has work been done? No.** The chamber is a constant-volume chamber, so \(\Delta V = 0\) and

\(W = p\,\Delta V = 0\)

The system does no work on its environment, and none is done on it. This is an isochoric process.

**(c) What is the sign of \(\Delta U\)? Negative.** Substituting the two results into the first law,

\(\Delta U = Q - W = Q - 0 = Q\)

and since \(Q\) is negative, \(\Delta U\) is **negative**. The internal energy of the fuel and oxygen system **decreases**. The energy released by the combustion does not stay in the system: with no work possible, the whole of it escapes as heat into the water bath, which is why the water warms up. The system ends with less internal energy than it began with, by exactly the amount of heat the water gained.

**Worth comparing with the rigid *insulated* cylinder of part (i).** There the chamber was also rigid, so \(W = 0\) again — but it was insulated, so \(Q = 0\) as well and \(\Delta U = 0\). Here the chamber is rigid but **not** insulated, so the same released energy leaks away as heat and \(\Delta U\) is negative. The one difference in the boundary changes the answer completely.

**How to draw the diagram.** Take the **volume \(V\) along the horizontal axis** and the **pressure \(p\) along the vertical axis**; such a graph is the \(p\)-\(V\) diagram, or indicator diagram, of the system. Mark the initial state as a point \(1\) at \((V_1,\ p_1)\) and the final state as a point \(2\) at \((V_2,\ p_2)\), and join them by the curve the process actually follows. **Put an arrowhead on the curve pointing from 1 to 2** — the direction in which the curve is traversed is what fixes the sign of the work, and a curve drawn without an arrow does not say which of the two works it represents. Finally drop vertical dashed lines from \(1\) and \(2\) down to the \(V\) axis and shade the strip bounded by the curve, the two dashed lines and the \(V\) axis.

**Why the shaded strip is the work.** The work done by the system in an infinitesimal change is \(dW = p\,dV\), so over the whole process

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2} p\,dV\)

This integral is exactly the **area under the \(p\)-\(V\) curve** between the two volumes. So the shaded area gives the magnitude of the work, and the direction of the arrow gives its sign.

**Positive work — draw the arrow pointing to the RIGHT.** Then \(V_2 > V_1\): the gas **expands**. Every element \(dV\) is positive, so \(W = \int p\,dV\) is **positive**. The system does work **on** its surroundings — it loses energy in pushing the piston out. On the diagram, an area swept from left to right is counted **positive**.

**Negative work — draw a second curve with the arrow pointing to the LEFT.** Then \(V_2 < V_1\): the gas is **compressed**. Every element \(dV\) is negative, so \(W\) is **negative**. Work is done **on** the system by the surroundings. The same area, swept from right to left, is counted **negative**.

If the two states lie on one vertical line, \(V_1 = V_2\), no area is enclosed at all and \(W = 0\) — no work is done in a constant-volume process, because there is no displacement.

**Example of positive work — expansion at constant pressure.** A gas heated in a cylinder at constant pressure pushes the piston out from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\). Its \(p\)-\(V\) curve is a horizontal straight line traversed to the right, the shaded area is a rectangle, and

\(W = p\,(V_2 - V_1) > 0\)

Water boiling at atmospheric pressure into steam, so that the steam pushes the surrounding air back, is a familiar instance.

**Example of negative work — the compression stroke of an engine.** The piston is pushed in, the volume falls from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\) and the curve is traversed to the left, so \(W\) is negative. In a diesel engine this compression is adiabatic: with \(Q = 0\), the first law gives \(\Delta U = -W\), so the negative work makes \(\Delta U\) positive and the mixture heats up enough to ignite.

**Setting up the two systems.** In each cooker the **system** is the food together with the water and air enclosed with it; the walls and lid of the cooker are its **boundary**; and everything outside — the Sun and the open air in one case, the burner and the kitchen in the other — is its **environment**. In both, cooking means raising the internal energy of that system until the food is cooked.

**Similarities**

1. Both are thermodynamic systems in which the food is cooked by **supplying heat from the environment**, so \(Q\) is positive for the system in both.
2. The first law \(Q = \Delta U + W\) governs both. In each, the heat supplied raises the internal energy of the contents, and hence their temperature, and any part of it that is not stored is spent as work.
3. In both, the energy flows in because the environment (the absorbing surface heated by the Sun, or the flame under the base) is at a **higher temperature than the contents**; cooking stops as soon as that supply of heat stops.
4. Both are built to **cut the loss of heat** back to the surroundings — the one by enclosing the vessel behind a transparent cover, the other by a tightly sealed lid — so both cook with less energy than an open vessel.
5. Both behave as **closed systems** for most of the process: energy crosses the boundary but the contents do not escape.

**Differences**

| Property | Solar cooker | Pressure cooker |
|---|---|---|
| Source of energy | Solar **radiation** — energy arrives as electromagnetic radiation and is absorbed by the dark inner surface; no fuel is burnt | A **burner** in thermal contact with the base — energy arrives mainly by conduction from a flame, and fuel is consumed |
| Pressure of the system | Stays essentially at **atmospheric** pressure, so the change is close to **isobaric**, \(\Delta p \approx 0\) | The lid is sealed, so steam accumulates and the pressure rises **well above atmospheric** until the weight lifts |
| Work done | The contents may expand against the atmosphere, so the system does some positive work, \(W = p\,\Delta V > 0\) | While the lid is sealed the volume is essentially fixed, so \(W \approx 0\) and nearly all the heat goes into \(\Delta U\) (**isochoric**) |
| Temperature reached | Limited to about \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\) while water is present, since water boils away at atmospheric pressure | The raised pressure raises the boiling point of the water above \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\), so the food reaches a **higher temperature** |
| Speed of cooking | **Slow** — \(Q\) is small and depends on the sunshine available, so it is weather-dependent and cannot be controlled | **Fast** — \(Q\) is large and can be regulated at the burner; the higher temperature also cooks the food faster |
| Exchange of matter | A **closed** system: energy crosses the boundary, matter does not | Closed until the safety valve lifts; once steam escapes it behaves as an **open** system, losing matter as well as energy |

**In short:** both are systems that cook by absorbing heat, but they differ in *how* the heat arrives (radiation against conduction from a flame), and in *which* state variable is held fixed — the solar cooker works at constant pressure and does work as it expands, while the sealed pressure cooker works at nearly constant volume, does almost no work, and converts its heat into internal energy and a rise in pressure, which is what lets it cook above \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\).

[Note: the one step above that this chapter does not itself establish is that raising the pressure raises the boiling point of water. That relation comes from the study of change of state under pressure; this chapter supplies everything else used here — the system/boundary/environment picture, the first law, and the isobaric and isochoric conditions.]
